archetype.name: Rebuilding (QB audition)
archetype.definition: A first-year-coach team whose rebuilt passing game was undone by a leaky defense, and which has now handed the rest of the season to Fernando Mendoza to see what it has.

report.headline: A real offensive revival, wasted by a defense that can't get off the field
report.take:
Las Vegas is two teams stacked on top of each other. The first is Klint Kubiak's offense, a genuine turnaround: a unit that ranked dead last in offensive EPA in 2025 (-0.192, scoring 14.2 points a game) climbed to the middle of the league (0.012, 16th), and Kirk Cousins' passing game ran at 0.092 EPA a dropback, 13th. The second is a defense that has slid from 7th in EPA allowed in 2023 to 27th now, allowing more points per game than anyone. The early wins over Miami, the Chargers and New Orleans came against offenses that rank 28th, 32nd and 22nd today. Once the schedule turned to Kansas City, Buffalo, the Rams and the 49ers, the defense stopped holding up and the Raiders won only once more.

The losses are worth reading closely, because the offense was not the problem in most of them. Cousins posted pass EPA of 8.9 against Kansas City, 7.5 at New England and 9.2 against Buffalo, and lost all three. The defense is a strange boom-or-bust unit: it creates pressure on 27.2% of dropbacks (3rd) and has 14 takeaways (4th), yet it allows a 47.8% success rate (31st) and is the league's worst at defending short passes. It wins the snaps where the rush gets home and loses nearly all the rest. Opponents get easy completions underneath, move the chains, and finish in the red zone 71.1% of the time.

The 4-7 record is roughly honest. The point differential is -52, which implies 3.4 wins, so if anything they have been slightly fortunate, and their turnover margin is only +3. The bigger shift is the quarterback switch. With Mendoza starting the last two weeks, the passing game went negative (-7.1 and -1.5 pass EPA) and protection collapsed: 6 sacks against Seattle and 5 at Denver. That came from a line whose 3.2% sack rate ranks 2nd for the season. Most of that rank was built with Cousins, and it now looks like a product of his quick decisions as much as the blocking.

The run game sits underneath all of it. The Raiders are last in yards per carry (3.01), yards before contact (1.39) and run success rate, yet they still pass less than expected (-3.4, 25th). Running backs are being asked to beat defenders in the backfield on early downs, which leaves a young quarterback in obvious passing situations. Until that changes, the rest of the season is about how Mendoza develops, not the standings.

strengths.title: A pass rush that wrecks drives
strengths.body: The front gets home: 27.2% pressure (3rd) and a 16.8% QB hit rate (8th), and that pressure feeds 14 takeaways, 4th in the league. This is the one defensive trait that has held up against good and bad offenses alike. It is under threat right now because four interior linemen are on the injury report.

strengths.title: A passing game rebuilt from scratch
strengths.body: Kubiak took an offense that was 32nd in EPA last season and made it league-average overall, with an above-average dropback game. Brock Bowers, Tre Tucker and Ashton Jeanty out of the backfield gave Cousins a spread-out target tree, and the Raiders put up big passing EPA even in losses. Whether the scheme carries over to Mendoza is the open question.

strengths.title: Clean, disciplined football
strengths.body: They are 3rd-fewest in penalties per game and 2nd in line penalties, and special teams add value (1.2 EPA a game, 7th). Discipline tends to be a coaching trait that lasts, and it matters most for a team living in close games.

concerns.title: A defense that can't stop the routine play
concerns.body: Allowing the 31st-ranked success rate and the worst EPA on short passes means opponents can march without needing explosives, and they finish drives at the 28th-ranked red-zone rate. That is a structural flaw, not bad luck: the rush either gets home or the coverage gives up easy completions behind it. It has sunk them against good offenses all year.

concerns.title: A dead run game they keep feeding
concerns.body: Last in yards per carry and in yards before contact means the blocking is losing at the point of attack before the back ever gets a chance. Despite that, the Raiders run more than expected. That puts the offense behind the chains and shortens possessions: their time of possession ranks 30th.

concerns.title: Protection collapsed with the QB change
concerns.body: Cousins rarely took sacks. Mendoza was sacked 6 times by Seattle and 5 times at Denver, so the line's elite season sack rate no longer describes the current offense. Some of that is a new starter holding the ball, and some of it may be a line that was protected by its veteran quarterback.

trend.note: A strong September against weak offenses gave way to a run of losses once the schedule stiffened, and the Raiders have failed to cover in each of the last four. Mendoza's two starts produced the two worst passing games of the year by EPA.

nextGame.headline: Raiders' pass rush meets the league's leakiest pass protection
nextGame.body:
Cleveland is 6-4 but plays more like Las Vegas than its record suggests. Its net EPA ranks 21st, its point differential is negative, and a .714 record in one-score games plus 1.62 wins over expected carry most of the gap. The Browns' offense scores 17.9 points a game (29th) behind a line that has allowed 38 sacks and the worst sack rate in football. That sets up the Raiders' best unit, the pass rush, against Cleveland's worst. The problem runs the other way too: the Browns' defense is 11th in EPA allowed with 26 sacks (3rd), and it faces a Mendoza-led offense that just took 11 sacks across two starts. The Book has Cleveland -4.5 with a 41.5 total, which points to a low-scoring game decided by who survives their own protection problems.

Availability leans on both trenches. Brock Bowers (ankle), the Raiders' target leader, is listed out, but Kubiak said he is optimistic about a return for this game, and his presence changes how much Mendoza has to hold the ball. The defensive interior is thin: Tonka Hemingway is out, and Adam Butler (concussion), Tim Keenan III and JJ Pegues are all questionable after leaving the Denver game. That could blunt the interior rush that makes the matchup with Cleveland's line so appealing. For the Browns, starting safety Ronnie Hickman (99% of snaps) is out with a concussion, a real hole in a back end that has been good against deep throws.

waysToWin.title: Pressure turns Cleveland drives into sacks
waysToWin.body: The Raiders' 3rd-ranked pressure rate against a line that gives up a sack on more than a tenth of dropbacks is the clearest mismatch on the field. Drive-killing sacks and forced throws also play into a defense that has collected takeaways all year. This edge depends on enough healthy interior linemen to keep the rush coming.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yardage
waysToWin.body: Cleveland commits more penalties than any team, while the Raiders are among the cleanest and own a top-10 special teams unit. In a game priced around 41 points, free first downs and field position can decide it.

waysToWin.title: Break tackles for chunk runs
waysToWin.body: The Browns miss more tackles than anyone and allow the highest explosive-run rate in the league. Even a run game as stuck as Las Vegas' could pop a few big gains through Jeanty and take pressure off Mendoza. The Raiders did post their best rushing EPA of the year at Denver last week.

waysToLose.title: Mendoza gets buried by the rush
waysToLose.body: Cleveland's pass rush ranks 3rd in sacks, and Mendoza has been taken down at a rate the offense can't survive. If the Raiders run on early downs and stall, Mendoza will face obvious passing downs, and the game could look like the Seattle loss.

waysToLose.title: Short completions bleed the clock
waysToLose.body: Even a weak offense can live on the Raiders' worst-in-league short-pass defense, chaining first downs and scoring in the red zone, where Las Vegas allows touchdowns 71.1% of the time. A thinned defensive interior makes it worse.

waysToLose.title: A one-score finish goes Cleveland's way
waysToLose.body: Cleveland has made a habit of winning close games, while the Raiders can't run to protect a lead and rank near the bottom in time of possession. A tight fourth quarter favors the team that has been closing these out.

nextGame.watch: How quickly Mendoza gets the ball out on early downs. If the sack total stays near the last two weeks, the Raiders' own pass rush can't make up the difference.

restOfSeason.body:
The rest of the schedule is split: three listed games against bad teams (the 1-9 Chargers and Titans at home, the 3-8 Cardinals on the road) and two against the AFC West's 8-2 leaders, Denver and Kansas City. That makes 6-11 a realistic floor and 7-10 a plausible ceiling, but the more meaningful question is what Mendoza looks like by January. The pass rush and the discipline should hold up. The takeaway pace and the elite sack-rate allowed are the most likely numbers to regress, and the second has arguably already broken with the quarterback change.

Scoring should drop from Cousins-era levels unless Mendoza finds the rhythm that Bowers and Tucker can give him. The defense should look better on paper against the Chargers' and Titans' offenses, but the core problem of short completions and red-zone touchdowns will resurface against Denver and Kansas City. Expect a team that wins the games it should and gets outclassed by the division leaders.
swingFactors: Mendoza's pocket management and sack rate
Bowers' health and the defensive-tackle injury cluster
Whether Kubiak shifts from a futile run game to the pass

confidence.note: Nine Cousins starts give a clear read on the team, but only two Mendoza starts define what it is now.
